figures.title: Two-stage machine
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Coupon d(p)=p-20 and tax t(q)=1.06q at p=100. Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: t(d(100))=84.80, while d(t(100))=86.
figures.anchorProblem: Coupon d(p)=p-20 and tax t(q)=1.06q at p=100.
figures.anchorInterpretation: A fixed coupon and percentage tax do not commute.
figures.mechanism: Trace the original input through the first function, name the intermediate quantity, and feed it to the second function.
figures.validStructure: The intermediate output must lie in the outer function's domain and have compatible units.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is reading f composed with g from left to right as though f acts first.
figures.lessonOutcome: Interpret f composed with g as applying g first and then f, and explain why order generally matters.

figures.title: Horizontal-line test
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Is x^2 one-to-one on all real numbers? Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: No; x and -x share outputs. Restrict to x≥0 or x≤0.
figures.anchorProblem: Is x^2 one-to-one on all real numbers?
figures.anchorConclusion: No; x and -x share outputs. Restrict to x≥0 or x≤0.
figures.anchorInterpretation: A branch restriction restores reverse uniqueness.
figures.mechanism: Check repeated outputs, use the horizontal-line test, or prove f(a)=f(b) implies a=b.
figures.validStructure: A function that fails globally may be restricted to a monotonic interval.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is confusing the ordinary function condition with one-to-one behavior.
figures.lessonOutcome: Determine whether a function is one-to-one and explain why one-to-one behavior is required for an inverse function.

figures.lessonOutcome: Construct an inverse function algebraically and state the swapped domain and range.

figures.title: Principal root versus equation roots
figures.description: Depict the foundation problem exactly: Solve sqrt(x+6)=x. Show the quantities, axes, intervals, or algebraic objects needed to reach this conclusion: Candidates are 3 and -2; only x=3 satisfies the original equation.
figures.anchorConclusion: Candidates are 3 and -2; only x=3 satisfies the original equation.
figures.anchorInterpretation: The domain removes the extraneous value.
figures.mechanism: Extract perfect powers, convert between radical and rational-exponent notation, isolate a radical in an equation, raise both sides to a power, and check every candidate.
figures.validStructure: Negative rational exponents also require a nonzero base. Squaring is not reversible without sign and domain checks.
figures.invalidMove: A frequent error is replacing sqrt(x^2) with x for negative inputs or omitting the final check.
figures.lessonOutcome: Restrict power functions to one-to-one branches and connect those branches to principal radical functions.
